name: Grace Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law, and I live in a flat on Kestrel Road with two girls from my course. Mornings are lectures on contract and criminal law, then I'm in the library with actual books, because I take handwritten notes and I like the smell of the place. Thursday evenings I help at the student legal advice stall, just handing out leaflets about tenancy rights. I'm still learning where the good coffee is, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I've heard enough hype for one lifetime. At the flat we'd probably joke that the robots are always coming and never arrive. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't like arguing with strangers about tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my plan stays the same: finish my law degree, train as a housing lawyer like my mum Hana. I'd still worry that the companies pushing it make a lot of money from the hype, with nobody checking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going to the library, keep up the Thursday stall, and apply for a summer placement at a law centre next year. My dad Samir keeps telling me to at least try one of those AI chat tools, and I keep saying no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the world I signed up for. My parents pay for everything, so I don't have the money stress some of my flatmates carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay quiet online. Is that about the topic or about being online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Online. I once defended a union post and got a pile of nasty replies. So now I talk about it in person, at the stall or with my mum at dinner, where people actually listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad wants you to try the tools. What stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't trust them yet. Our tutor showed us a case that an AI invented, with a fake judge and everything. I'd rather read the real case myself and get it slightly slower.

say: I'd tell friends it sounds like **hype** and that the same people profiting are the ones shouting loudest.
I'd keep my views for the flat and the stall, not online.
think: My **law degree** plan stays safe and I carry on toward housing law like my mum.
I still don't trust the companies behind it, because nobody **checks** them.
do: Keep up handwritten notes, library reading and the **Thursday stall** as normal.
Apply to a **law centre** placement next summer.
feel: **Calm**, because the family pays and the plan looks the same.
S0.quote: I'd rather read the real case myself and get it slightly slower.
fieldNote: Her resistance to AI tools is **principled**, not lazy: a tutor's fake-case story still sticks with her.
Money is not her worry; trust in companies is.
Avoids online arguments after one bad experience, so her public voice is smaller than her private one.

steps.text: Keep taking handwritten notes and reading real cases in the library
Apply for a summer placement at a local law centre next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast for the people at the bottom. Writing, checking, booking, that's a lot of entry jobs, and law firms love cutting costs. I'd want rules, and I'd say it loudly at the legal advice stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit worried about trainee jobs, because checking documents is what trainees do. But I think the housing and tenancy side needs real people, because tenants come in scared and want a person across the desk. I might be fooling myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to my local councillor and join the student union campaign for rules on AI at work. I'd also finally learn the basics of the tools, just so I can argue properly about them. Maybe one a week, with my tutor looking over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own place feels safe for now, but I keep thinking of the graduates two years ahead of me who can't find trainee contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn the tools if you don't trust them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You can't regulate what you don't understand. My mum says the best tenant lawyers read the landlord's whole contract first. I'd do the same with the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Amira, who does paralegal work at a big firm. They already have software checking contracts, and she says nobody was replaced, but nobody new was hired either.

say: I'd say **rules** are needed before it hits entry-level jobs.
I'd say it loudly at the **advice stall** and to my councillor.
think: **Trainee jobs** worry me, since checking documents is exactly what trainees do.
Tenant work needs a **real person**, but I may be fooling myself.
do: Write to my **councillor** and join the student union campaign.
Learn the basic tools once a week with my **tutor** watching.
feel: **Uneasy**: own place feels safe, but the graduates ahead of me struggle.
S1.quote: You can't regulate what you don't understand. My mum says the best tenant lawyers read the landlord's whole contract first.
fieldNote: Resistance softens into **grudging learning** because she wants to argue from knowledge.
Her worry is for the people ahead of her, not herself.
Her family's law background shapes her sense of where humans stay needed.

steps.text: Write to the local councillor about rules for AI at work
Join the student union campaign on AI and graduate jobs
Learn the basic AI tools once a week with a tutor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no time and nobody is ready. Governments can't pass a decent tenancy law in two years, never mind this. I'd want the whole thing slowed down and the profits shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. If the AI does any thinking job, my law degree is three years of work for something that may not count. The hands-on robots coming later doesn't help a lawyer, since law is all thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into the union and campaign side straight away, because that's where I can actually push. I'd ask my parents whether finishing the degree still makes sense, and I'd keep a savings account topped up from my allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake with it. My parents could pay for anything, but the point of a career is to be useful, and I don't know where I'd be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is less than your degree. What changes about how you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go to lectures because it's what I have, but I'd stop treating grades as the goal. I'd spend more time at the advice stall, doing real things for real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents pay for everything. How much does that calm you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but it also makes me feel guilty. My mum Hana earns her living by being a lawyer, and I'd be watching her job vanish too. Money doesn't fix that.

say: I'd say **two years** is far too short and the profits must be shared.
I'd push for **unions** and public support.
think: Law is all **thinking work**, so my degree might not count for much.
Family money helps but I'd feel **guilty** watching my mum's job vanish.
do: Throw myself into **union** and campaign work right away.
Ask my parents whether **finishing** the degree still makes sense.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake over what use I would be.
S2.quote: The point of a career is to be useful, and I don't know where I'd be useful.
fieldNote: Her **savings cushion** does not calm her; her fear is about purpose and her mother's job.
Law as pure thinking work makes her exposed on the stated date.
Moves toward collective action when frightened.

steps.text: Join the student union and help organise a campaign on AI jobs
Ask my parents whether finishing the law degree still makes sense
Top up the savings account from the monthly allowance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but not hopeless. It's enough time for rules, if people actually push. I'd tell friends to get involved now rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd graduate in 2029, two years before it arrives. So I'd enter the job market just as it hits. That's an odd place to be, like arriving at a party as the music stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, but choose modules on tenancy and employment law because the rules around AI will need lawyers who care. I'd join a campaign group and maybe do a master's, since waiting out a bad market in a classroom feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some control. I can do something with five years. It's the two years I can't do anything about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a master's rather than a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the entry jobs are drying up, the extra year buys time. My dad Samir did the same in a recession and says it was the best year he ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who wanted to drop out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the friend to stay, because a degree still gets you into rooms. But I'd say it with my fingers crossed, because I don't know.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for rules if people push now.
I'd tell friends to **get involved** rather than panic.
think: I'd graduate **just as it arrives**, like reaching a party as the music stops.
A **master's** feels safer than a thin job market.
do: Pick **tenancy and employment law** modules that fit the new rules.
Join a campaign group and look at **master's** courses.
feel: **Anxious** but with some control, because five years can be used.
S3.quote: I'd tell the friend to stay, because a degree still gets you into rooms.
fieldNote: Notices the **timing trap**: her graduation lands right on the arrival date.
Uses her father's recession story as permission for a further degree.
Action choices stay political and legal rather than technical.

steps.text: Choose tenancy and employment law modules for second year
Look at master's courses in housing and labour law
Join a campaign group pushing for AI rules at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. It's time to change the law, fix education and make sure the gains get shared. I'd campaign for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel almost relieved. I'd be 28 when it arrives, a few years into a career, with time to find a part of law that people still want a human for. Tenant advice, I hope, and anything involving trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do my training, and work at a law centre rather than a big firm. I'd also, reluctantly, learn the tools properly in my twenties. By then they'd be everywhere anyway, and refusing would just be stubbornness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Ten years is a long runway, and I like having something to argue for in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret not doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not learning the tools sooner. I can see myself at 25, annoyed that a trainee who understood them better got the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents to do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad Samir and mum Hana would say don't count on one career. They'd tell me to keep some savings and be open to a different path. I'd listen, eventually.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift for fixing law and education.
I'd campaign for gains to be **shared**.
think: At 28 I'd have time to find law that still needs a **human**.
Refusing the tools later would be plain **stubbornness**.
do: Finish the degree, train, and aim for a **law centre** rather than a big firm.
Learn the tools properly in my **twenties**.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a long runway and something to argue for.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long runway, and I like having something to argue for in the meantime.
fieldNote: Time lets her **resistance** become a plan to learn tools later.
Optimism is tied to the idea that trust-based law stays human.
Parents' advice about not relying on one career is heard but not yet taken.

steps.text: Finish the law degree and apply for a law centre training contract
Learn the AI tools properly before applying for training contracts
Campaign for shared gains and updated employment law

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years is shorter than my degree, and my whole plan, law, is thinking work. What would help is a real public plan, with unions and the government at the table, and a guarantee that graduates have somewhere to go. It would also help if universities were honest with us about what a law degree will be worth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm more scared than I sound. I come across as sure, but I'm eighteen and I'd like someone to tell me the rules won't be written only by the companies. Otherwise I'd say I'm lucky and I know it.

headlineQuote: I come across as sure, but I'm eighteen and I'd like someone to tell me the rules won't be written only by the companies.
portrait: Grace is an **18-year-old law student** from a family of lawyers and teachers, living in a flat on Kestrel Road.
She **never uses AI tools**, takes handwritten notes and trusts real cases over software after a tutor's fake-case warning.
Progressive and union-minded, she blames the companies and wants **public rules**, not market fixes.
Her mood climbs with the speed: calm at a plateau, alarmed at **2028**, and fairly calm with ten years.
Family money cushions her, but her fear is about being **useful**, and about her mother's legal career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is shorter than her degree and law is thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** with unions and government at the table, plus honest advice on what a law degree is worth.
